lesson.title: The Field's Common Language: The DSM
lesson.summary: The DSM, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, is the classification system most widely used for diagnosing psychological disorders in the United States, providing specific criteria intended to make diagnosis more consistent across clinicians.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter established that defining a psychological disorder is genuinely difficult, resting on some combination of distress, dysfunction, deviance, and danger without any one criterion working perfectly alone. The DSM is one major attempt to turn that difficult, general definition into something usable in day-to-day clinical and research practice. Published by the American Psychiatric Association, worth noting is that this organization is often abbreviated APA, which is also the abbreviation for the separate American Psychological Association, a common and understandable point of confusion, the DSM lists specific disorders along with the symptoms, duration, and degree of impairment required to diagnose each one.

The current edition is the DSM-5-TR, a text revision published in 2022 that updated the DSM-5, originally published in 2013. A typical DSM entry for a given disorder lists a set of possible symptoms and specifies how many must be present, for how long, and requires that the symptoms cause meaningful distress or impairment in functioning, tying the manual's criteria directly back to the distress and dysfunction concepts from the prior chapter. The core purpose is reliability: helping two different clinicians evaluating the same patient reach the same diagnosis, which matters enormously for treatment planning, research comparability, insurance coverage, and legal proceedings.

The DSM has changed substantially across its editions, both in what it includes and how it is organized. For example, the earlier DSM-IV used a multiaxial system that separated clinical disorders from personality disorders, medical conditions, and overall functioning onto different axes, a structure the DSM-5 dropped in favor of a single, nonaxial diagnostic listing. The manual's contents have also tracked shifting scientific evidence and social understanding over time, and specific diagnoses have been added, removed, or redefined as that evidence and consensus changed. Revisions are developed by committees of researchers and clinicians reviewing the available scientific literature, but the process, and individual diagnostic decisions within it, have also been genuinely debated and criticized within the field, an extension of the same underlying tension already present in defining disorder itself.

The DSM is not the only major classification system in use. The next chapter turns to the ICD, a system with a different history, a different publisher, and a much broader international reach.
